PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Bottom line

The Seller's package departs from our playbook on almost every term that matters. If we accepted it, we would buy Paperbark with heavily reduced warranty protection, no fraud protection, and several value leaks: Bluefen, Riverlark, the bonuses and title. **We should reject the package as a whole and return a mark-up based on our starting positions.** No playbook fallback should be offered, because none has been authorised.

---

## 1. How the package is framed

Before turning to the clauses, the cover note uses several framing devices that we should not accept:

- **"[STANDARD] – reviewed and cleared by both sides; focus only on [OPEN]."** The Seller applied these labels itself. Nothing in it is marked [OPEN], so the instruction would mean reviewing nothing. I have reviewed every clause.
- **"Settled at principal level… FINAL and not intended to be re-opened."** We have no record of any such agreement. More importantly, two of these positions are playbook fallbacks: the 20% cap and the 18-month period. Both require **prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft**, and none has been given. A statement in a counterparty's cover email cannot stand in for that authority.
- **"Market context" (10–20% caps, ~1% baskets, 12–18 months, buyer-knowledge).** This is the Seller's advocacy, not evidence. Our positions are set by the playbook.
- **"The parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package."** We have not.

**The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts its summary.** For example:
- The summary says Bluefen is "addressed"; the letter says there is **no** consent and **no** evidence that the conditions are satisfied.
- The summary says the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller"; the letter confirms they are **not in the funds flow** and that on-costs are unaddressed.

I suggest Amelia Frost replies at principal level that no positions are agreed and no fallback authority exists.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### A. Liability architecture (highest priority)

| # | Topic | Seller position | Playbook | Assessment / pushback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **General cap (cl 12.1)** | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m | This is our fallback, used without authority. **Hold 25%.** Do not reveal that a fallback exists. |
| 2 | **De minimis (cl 12.2)** | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 | Five times our position. **Reject.** |
| 3 | **Basket (cl 12.2)** | AUD 250,000, excess only | AUD 50,000, first-dollar once exceeded | Five times the amount, and a deductible instead of a tipping basket. With the higher de minimis, this would exclude a large share of realistic warranty claims. **Reject both elements.** |
| 4 | **General claims period (cl 12.3)** | 18 months | 24 months | Fallback without authority. **Hold 24 months.** |
| 5 | **"Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13)** | Universal default | Separate categories; no hidden override | **This is a significant hidden override.** It would pull Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenant and payment claims, and potentially fraud, into the general regime unless each is carved out expressly. **Delete it.** Reverse the default so the general limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. |
| 6 | **Fundamental / Title** | Same caps and time limits as general warranties, "for administrative simplicity" | 100% cap, at least 6 years, outside basket, de minimis and knowledge bar | Capping title at AUD 4.8m on a AUD 24m share purchase would leave us exposed if the Seller does not own what it is selling. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason. **Reject outright.** |
| 7 | **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)** | Universal | Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of everything, to the maximum extent enforceable | As drafted, this purports to cap and time-bar fraud claims and to use non-reliance against misrepresentation claims. **This is non-negotiable. No one on our side may waive it.** Insert an overriding carve-out in each of cl 9.3, 12, 12.8, 13 and 20.5. Also note the compounding effect of #5. |

### B. Disclosure and knowledge

| # | Topic | Seller position | Playbook | Assessment / pushback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | **General disclosure (DL 1.1, 1.2)** | Whole data room (DD-002 to DD-012), Accounts, statutory registers, public records | Specific fair disclosure only | **Reject DL 1.1 and 1.2 in full.** Disclosure must be specific and fair against identified warranties. It must be detailed enough for us to assess the nature and scope of the matter. |
| 9 | **Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3)** | No claim for anything the Buyer *or its advisers* knew, or that was discoverable from the data room or public records | Delete blanket exclusions. Any qualifier needs named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities | **Delete.** Read with DL 1.1, this clause would largely cancel the warranties. Everything in the data room would count as "known", and the specific indemnities would be undermined, since a specific indemnity exists because we know about the issue. |
| 10 | **Non-admission (DL 1.4)** | No admission of breach, liability, materiality etc. | — | Generally acceptable as a disclosure-letter convention. Confirm it cannot be used to narrow any specific indemnity, covenant or condition. |
| 11 | **Staleness** | DL dated as at 22 Sept 2026 | — | It is now 5 Nov 2026. Require an updated disclosure position and a bring-down mechanism. Any new disclosures should not cure warranty breaches without our consent. |

### C. Completion protections and value leakage

**12. Bluefen consent (cl 3 / 6.3): high priority.**
- **Why it matters:** Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m, or roughly 30%, of FY26 revenue, and has a change-control clause (11.2) with conditions (11.3).
- **The Seller's draft is weak on this.** It offers only reasonable endeavours, and treats the condition as satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent". That would be met even if the 11.3 conditions were never satisfied.
- **The Disclosure Letter confirms the gap:** there is no final consent and no evidence of the conditions.
- **What to require:**
  - A Condition Precedent requiring an effective consent **and** documentary evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied before Completion.
  - Waivable by the Buyer only.
  - A long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
  - A stronger effort standard, such as best or all reasonable endeavours, with reporting obligations.

**13. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7): high priority.**
- **The exposure:** about AUD 3.2m is outstanding. There is a change-control clause (8.1) and a discharge clause (9.2), and the facility has not been repaid. A "release to be provided following Completion" leaves us exposed to the security and to a change-control default on Day 1.
- **What to require:**
  - A current payout letter.
  - Repayment made **directly from Completion funds** to Riverlark.
  - Executed deeds of release and PPSR/security discharges delivered at Completion.
  - Treatment as Debt in the debt-free/cash-free price mechanics.
- **Fallback:** a post-Completion release is acceptable only with an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark **and** Amelia Frost's approval. We should not offer it now.
- **Linked point:** check whether Riverlark's security extends to the **shares** being sold. See also Title, item 18.

**14. Employee bonuses (DD-005, AUD 420,000): high priority.**
- **The problem:** the funds flow silently excludes them. "A matter for the Seller" does not protect us. These are Company obligations that would fall due on Completion, so the Company, and therefore we, would bear them after Completion. The Disclosure Letter also does not address payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs.
- **What to require:** either a specific funds-flow line item, deducted from the price and paid through payroll, or express Seller funding. In both cases include all triggered on-costs. Back this with an indemnity and leakage protection.

### D. Specific risk items

**15. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1).**
- **The problem:** an indemnity limited to "the specific SOW3 payment" is too narrow. The real risk is ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials, since transfer depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee (DD-004 cl 7.3). Third-party claims and remediation costs are also uncovered.
- **What to require:**
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover title to and use of the SOW3 Project Materials, Ironquay claims, and remediation.
  - **Preserve the SOW3 cure:** before Completion, evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees plus a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay.
- **Caution:** the AUD 180,000 open in DD-010 is not independently verified in either direction. We should not assume it is owed, or that it has been paid. Ask for bank evidence or an Ironquay statement.

**16. Export/privacy incident (DD-006, cl 4.6 / Sched 6).**
- **The problem:** the Seller's statement that it is "not expected to be material" is an unsupported characterisation. Its own disclosure says the investigation is preliminary, and that access, scope and notification obligations are unestablished. The export may contain about 1,240 records.
- **What to require:** covenants to preserve all logs and evidence, complete a proper investigation, provide regular updates to us before Completion, and consult us on any notification decision. The Seller's characterisation should not qualify any warranty.
- **How to frame it:** we should **not** assert in either direction that there is a confirmed breach, harm, a notification duty or a loss figure. Any protection should be drafted without a numeric demand.

**17. Sandbar renewals (DD-008 / DD-011, 3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000).**
- **The problem:** the Seller asserts these are ordinary course, but its own disclosure says it does not state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
- **Our approach:** request the contracts and timing details and assess them. We should **not** accept the Seller's characterisation. Equally, under the playbook we should **not** treat them automatically as Debt or seek a price deduction. Decide once the facts are known.

**18. Title (DD-012).**
- **The problem:** a Company share register is an internal, Seller-supplied record. It is not independent proof of title.
- **What to require:**
  - Independent evidence: a current ASIC extract, share certificates, and confirmation that there are no encumbrances (PPSR search, and Riverlark releases if the shares are secured).
  - Evidence of authority and capacity, including Seller board approvals.
  - Fundamental title and capacity warranties on the separate regime in item 6.

**19. Tax and IP warranties.**
- **The problem:** the Seller says these are "settled under the general regime". They are **open**.
- **Our approach:** keep them as separate categories, outside the general cap, basket and time limit, to be negotiated. We should not assume unlimited liability or any agreed resolution.

**20. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower priority.**
- The disclosure describes a lease notification obligation and an assignment restriction, but no consent requirement triggered by the share sale.
- Verify both against the source documents.
- Add a covenant that the Seller gives any required notifications, and a warranty that no consent is required beyond those listed.

---

## 3. Summary of recommendations

**Reject outright (non-negotiable):**
1. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to fraud, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct. Insert overriding carve-outs throughout.
2. Fundamental and title warranties under the general cap and time limit. Require a 100% cap, at least six years, and exclusion from the basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
3. The "any limitation applies to all Claims" default. Reverse it.
4. Whole-data-room, public-register and Accounts general disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2).
5. The blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3).

**Restore our starting positions (no fallbacks; none authorised):**
6. A 25% / AUD 6.0m cap.
7. A AUD 5,000 de minimis and a AUD 50,000 tipping basket, recoverable from the first dollar.
8. A 24-month general claims period.

**Completion and value protection:**
9. Bluefen: a CP requiring effective consent plus evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied, with a stronger effort standard and a Buyer-only waiver.
10. Riverlark: a payout letter, direct repayment from Completion funds, and releases delivered at Completion.
11. Bonuses: AUD 420,000 plus on-costs, as a funds-flow line item or Seller-funded, with an indemnity.
12. Title: independent title, encumbrance and authority evidence beyond DD-012.

**Specific risk items:**
13. Ironquay: a broadened indemnity, preservation of the SOW3 cure, and verification of the AUD 180,000.
14. DD-006: covenants to preserve logs, investigate and report, with no characterisation either way.
15. Sandbar: information request and assessment, with no automatic Debt or price treatment.
16. Tax and IP: separate categories, flagged as open.
17. An updated disclosure letter as at a current date, with bring-down protections.

**Process:**
- Reply that no positions are agreed or final, and that every clause remains under review regardless of its label.
- Any move to the 20% cap, 18 months or a post-Completion Riverlark release requires Amelia Frost's prior written authority identifying the specific draft. Until then, our mark-up should not hint that fallbacks exist.

Once the team confirms these positions, I can prepare the issues list or the mark-up.

- **The problem:** an indemnity limited to "the specific SOW3 payment" is too narrow. The real risk is ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials, since transfer depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee (DD-004 cl 7.3). Third-party claims and remediation costs are also uncovered.

- **Caution:** the AUD 180,000 open in DD-010 is not independently verified in either direction. We should not assume it is owed, or that it has been paid. Ask for bank evidence or an Ironquay statement.

**16. Export/privacy incident (DD-006, cl 4.6 / Sched 6).**
- **The problem:** the Seller's statement that it is "not expected to be material" is an unsupported characterisation. Its own disclosure says the investigation is preliminary, and that access, scope and notification obligations are unestablished. The export may contain about 1,240 records.

**17. Sandbar renewals (DD-008 / DD-011, 3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000).**
- **The problem:** the Seller asserts these are ordinary course, but its own disclosure says it does not state whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
- **Our approach:** request the contracts and timing details and assess them. We should **not** accept the Seller's characterisation. Equally, under the playbook we should **not** treat them automatically as Debt or seek a price deduction. Decide once the facts are known.

**18. Title (DD-012).**
- **The problem:** a Company share register is an internal, Seller-supplied record. It is not independent proof of title.
- **What to require:**

  - Evidence of authority and capacity, including Seller board approvals.
  - Fundamental title and capacity warranties on the separate regime in item 6.

**19. Tax and IP warranties.**
- **The problem:** the Seller says these are "settled under the general regime". They are **open**.
- **Our approach:** keep them as separate categories, outside the general cap, basket and time limit, to be negotiated. We should not assume unlimited liability or any agreed resolution.

**20. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower priority.**
- The disclosure describes a lease notification obligation and an assignment restriction, but no consent requirement triggered by the share sale.
- Verify both against the source documents.
- Add a covenant that the Seller gives any required notifications, and a warranty that no consent is required beyond those listed.
